title: [chrony][BMC] System clock never converges after reboot/power-cycle on RTC-less BMC platforms (makestep is disabled)
author: william8545
body:
## Describe the bug

On SONiC BMC platforms without a battery-backed/persistent RTC (e.g. Aspeed AST2700-based BMC cards), the system clock comes up at a stale time after every boot and **never converges to the correct time**, even with NTP configured. `chronyc tracking` permanently reports `Leap status: Not synchronised`.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Deploy a SONiC BMC image on an Aspeed AST2700-based BMC (no persistent RTC).
2. Reboot — and in particular **power-cycle** — the BMC.
3. Log in and run `date` and `chronyc tracking`.

## Expected behavior

After boot (and once an NTP source is reachable), the system clock converges to the correct time within seconds.

## Actual behavior

The clock comes up weeks/months in the past and never corrects:

```
Reference ID    : 00000000 ()
Stratum         : 0
Ref time (UTC)  : Thu Jan 01 00:00:00 1970
Leap status     : Not synchronised
```

## Root cause analysis

**1. No persistent RTC on the BMC.** The on-SoC RTC is not battery-backed, so it resets on every power cycle. Kernel log at each boot:

```
aspeed-rtc 12c0f000.rtc: setting system clock to 1970-01-01T01:04:44 UTC (3884)
```

`systemd` then only advances the clock as far as its build epoch, so userspace sees a time pinned near the **image build date** (the offset from real time grows with image age).

**2. `makestep` is disabled in the shared chrony template** — `files/image_config/chrony/chrony.conf.j2`:

```jinja
# Disabled because we don't want chrony to do any clock steps; it should only slew
#makestep 1 3
```

This is intentional: the system clock is meant to only *slew* and never *step*, relying on a persistent RTC to provide correct time at boot. That is appropriate for switches but breaks on an RTC-less BMC — the boot-time offset is large, and chrony's default maximum slew rate (~8.3%, ≈83333 ppm) means correcting an offset of *N* seconds takes ≈ 12·*N* seconds, so a multi-week offset effectively never converges and each reboot resets it.

Background on why stepping is disabled (slew-only by design): see References.

> Note: a reachable, trustworthy NTP source is also required — `chrony` can only step/slew to a time it actually receives. That part is deployment-specific and separate from this issue.

## References

- HLD — SONiC Migration to Chrony: https://github.com/sonic-net/SONiC/blob/master/doc/ntp/migration-to-chrony.md
- HLD tracking issue: sonic-net/SONiC#1852
- ntpd → chrony PR: #20497
- Config template: `files/image_config/chrony/chrony.conf.j2`

#### Why I did it

For devices that may not have a reliable hardware clock (or don't have a hardware clock at all), systemd has a feature where it will update the system time with a more reasonable time if it sees that the time is wildly off or known to be incorrect. One of the sources of a reasonable time is an epoch file, at `/usr/lib/clock-epoch`. If the modification
time of the epoch file is greater than the system time, then it will update the system time to the modification time of the epoch file.

Fixes #27908

##### Work item tracking
- Microsoft ADO **(number only)**:

#### How I did it

Take advantage of this by writing an epoch file daily, so that if the device goes for a reboot (planned or unplanned), the system time is reasonably close. Also bind-mount that file from `/host` into `/usr/lib/clock-epoch`, so that it can be used across images.

#### How to verify it

Create the epoch file, set the time back to far before the epoch timestamp, reboot, and verify that the time from the epoch file is used.

comments.author: norimeher-arista
comments.body:
Hi @saiarcot895 , this fix only partially addresses the issue. It really depends on how long the device remains powered off, after a significant gap, chrony may take a long time to correct the clock by slewing.

I’m working on an HLD that would allow chrony to step the clock at most once during startup, then return to slew-only mode. I’d appreciate your thoughts on this approach. Thanks!

cc @vivekverma-arista @judyjoseph

comments.author: norimeher-arista
comments.body: Correction: The offset also depends on the interval since the last daily epoch update, not just the powered-off duration.

comments.author: saiarcot895
comments.body:
Hi @norimeher-arista, this change was never meant to completely fix the issue. It's meant to have it start from a slightly more correct time and thus take less time for it to get fully corrected/synchronized without (ideally) needing to resort to time jumps. This means instead of having it start from May 3, 2026 (the build time for systemd), it'll start from whenever the system was last powered off.

Automatic/uncontrolled time jumps (specifically the `makestep` command in the config) have been intentionally disabled due to issues seen in the past resulting in dataplane impact.

Two improvements I can see to reduce the diff:

1. Change the timer to be hourly instead of daily. I think in terms of disk writes, this should still be fine, as this would be an inode update.
2. Modify the sonic-mgmt add-topo step to do a makestep on the BMC. I know it's being done for DUT, but I'm not sure if that is being done for BMC as well.

comments.author: norimeher-arista
comments.body:
Ack that @saiarcot895. Thanks for a prompt reply back!

1.  Writing it hourly would certainly reduce the initial skew. However it doesn't fully mitigate the problem, does it?

2.  Performing makestep from the sonic-mgmt add-topo flow would help the test environment, but it would not address issues with deployed systems right.

 
 I agree that we should not restore a general persistent `makestep 1 3` directive in chrony.conf. As BMC doesn't work in the dataplane, stepping it would not directly alter the DUT clock or dataplane forwarding (Not completely sure, want to know your comments)

The proposed design is narrower:
- Enabled only on explicitly configured NetworkBmc platforms.
- Disabled on switch platforms.
- At most one explicit bootstrap-step attempt per BMC boot.
- Chrony restarts do not reopen the opportunity.
- No persistent makestep directive.


As a reference point, upstream OpenBMC enables systemd-timesyncd by default, and it immediately steps an accepted offset of 0.4 seconds or greater using ADJ_SETOFFSET: [configuration](https://github.com/openbmc/openbmc/blob/master/meta-phosphor/recipes-core/systemd/systemd_%25.bbappend#L2-L16) [timesyncd implementation](https://github.com/systemd/systemd/blob/v259.5/src/timesync/timesyncd-manager.c#L240-L293)
